subtopic_detail: One white pupil and one red pupil across several recent phone photographs in a thriving nine month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a nine month old girl in a general clinic. Her mother has brought her phone and shows you six photographs taken over the past two months, in which one pupil looks white while the other glows orange red.

The baby was born at term, feeds well and is tracking along the fiftieth centile for weight and length. She fixes on faces, follows a rolling ball across the room and reaches accurately for a small toy with either hand. There is no family history of childhood eye disease and no squint noticed by either parent.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the right and present on the left, no proptosis, no orbital swelling, corneal light reflex symmetrical, cover test reveals no shift on either side, anterior segments clear to penlight examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent referral to a paediatric ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthesia within one week
options.rationale: An absent red reflex in one eye is an urgent finding at any age and needs dilated examination under anaesthesia by a paediatric ophthalmologist, because the differential includes a tumour in which delay changes both survival and eye preservation. Normal visual behaviour does not soften the urgency, since a child with one working eye behaves normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Reassure the mother that asymmetric camera flash is common and review the child at her twelve month health check
options.rationale: Off axis flash can produce a false white pupil in a single photograph, but a reflex that is reproducibly absent on direct examination is not a photographic artefact. Reassurance without examination findings to support it is the main route by which these presentations are delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Request an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review the result at a routine clinic appointment in six weeks
options.rationale: Imaging is arranged by the ophthalmology service as part of a staging assessment, not as a filter before referral, and a six week routine loop wastes the interval that matters most. Ordering the scan first also risks a normal report being read as permission to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for refraction and occlusion therapy to prevent amblyopia in the affected eye
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once a structural cause has been excluded, and applying it first would treat a consequence while leaving the cause unexamined. Optometrists cannot perform the dilated examination under anaesthesia that this finding requires. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric vision screening)

options.text: Arrange a screening magnetic resonance scan of the brain and orbits before making any ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging has a role in assessing optic nerve and intracranial extension but follows the ophthalmic examination rather than preceding it, and in this age group it needs anaesthesia of its own. Sequencing it first adds a delay without changing the immediate pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

explanation.summary: The red reflex examination is part of every newborn check and every subsequent well child review in Australia, and its whole purpose is to detect opacity or mass in the visual axis before vision or life is threatened. An absent or asymmetric reflex carries a differential of retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinal detachment, persistent foetal vasculature and severe refractive error. Retinoblastoma is the reason the pathway is urgent rather than routine, because it is the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood and outcomes track tightly with time to diagnosis. Parents frequently present with photographs, and a reproducible white pupil across multiple images taken at different angles is a genuine finding rather than an artefact. Normal fixing and following in a child with one unaffected eye is expected and is never reassuring.
key_points: An absent unilateral red reflex requires paediatric ophthalmology assessment within days, not weeks
Normal visual behaviour is preserved when one eye is unaffected and does not exclude serious pathology
Repeated white pupil across several photographs taken at different angles argues against flash artefact
Definitive assessment is dilated examination under anaesthesia, with imaging arranged by the eye service
The differential spans retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinal detachment and persistent foetal vasculature
explanation.pearls: Around one in ten children with retinoblastoma present with squint rather than leukocoria, so a new squint after six months of age earns the same dilated examination that a white pupil does.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent eye discharge with marked lid swelling on day three of life after an unscreened pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a baby boy who is seventy hours old. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning she could barely part the lids to clean them.

He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery to a nineteen year old woman who booked late and declined the routine first trimester sexual health screen. He has fed hungrily throughout and has had six wet nappies in the past day. He is afebrile and handles normally when undressed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral lid oedema with thick yellow discharge reaccumulating within a minute of cleaning, conjunctival injection with chemosis, corneas clear to penlight, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash and no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Eye swab taken for Gram stain, bacterial culture and nucleic acid amplification testing, results pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly and review the baby on the postnatal ward the following morning
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone does not reach the systemic reservoir and does not prevent the corneal perforation that makes this presentation an emergency. Chloramphenicol drops are reasonable for a mild sticky eye later in the neonatal period, which is a different clinical picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and frequent saline eye irrigation, with maternal and partner contact tracing
options.rationale: Onset within the first five days with copious purulent discharge and marked lid oedema is managed as gonococcal ophthalmia until proven otherwise, which requires a systemic third generation cephalosporin plus mechanical clearance of the purulent load by irrigation. The mother and her partner need treatment and contact tracing because the baby is the sentinel case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral azithromycin for fourteen days and arrange community midwife review of the eyes every second day
options.rationale: Oral azithromycin is the treatment for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, which typically appears between days five and fourteen with less dramatic lid swelling and often a cough. Choosing it here covers the wrong organism during the window in which corneal damage occurs. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Observe with hourly saline cleaning alone and start antibiotics only once the swab results have become available
options.rationale: Irrigation is a necessary part of treatment but is not sufficient alone, and waiting for culture surrenders the day or two in which perforation can occur. Gram stain may return within hours but treatment starts on the clinical pattern rather than on the laboratory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal conjunctivitis)

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: This is the empirical regimen for undifferentiated early neonatal sepsis, but the baby is afebrile, feeding and systemically well with a localised picture, and neither agent reliably treats the organism in question. A broader workup would be triggered by systemic signs rather than by the eye findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Conjunctivitis in the first month of life is graded by time of onset and by the severity of the lid and discharge findings, because the two organisms that matter behave differently. Gonococcal disease presents hyperacutely in the first few days with copious pus and tense lid oedema, and it is the only cause that perforates the cornea within days. Chlamydial disease is commoner in Australia and presents in the second week with a more indolent watery then mucopurulent discharge, sometimes with an afebrile pneumonitis. Chemical irritation from birth prophylaxis and simple nasolacrimal duct obstruction make up most of the remaining presentations and need no antibiotics. Late booking with declined screening removes the antenatal safety net and shifts the pretest probability substantially.
key_points: Onset in the first five days with copious pus and tense lid oedema is treated as gonococcal until excluded
Systemic third generation cephalosporin plus saline irrigation is the treatment, not topical antibiotic alone
Chlamydial conjunctivitis appears from day five to fourteen and is treated with oral azithromycin
Corneal perforation is the complication that makes the gonococcal presentation a same day emergency
The neonate is the sentinel case, so maternal and partner treatment and contact tracing follow automatically
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial infection acquired at delivery can present as an afebrile staccato cough with tachypnoea at four to twelve weeks, long after the eyes have settled, so a past sticky eye is worth asking about in an afebrile infant with a persistent cough.

subtopic_detail: Painful restriction of eye movement with reduced colour vision emerging during treatment of a sinus infection
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a seven year old boy who has had a blocked nose and facial pain for eight days and was started on oral amoxicillin by his general practitioner three days ago. His mother brings him back because the swelling around his left eye has worsened since this morning and he now cries when he looks up.

He is alert, drinking and has had no vomiting. He has no history of trauma, insect bite or preceding skin lesion, and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense left periorbital swelling with erythema extending to the brow, globe displaced forwards and laterally, pain and limitation on upgaze and abduction, red desaturation on comparing a red object between the two eyes, visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/12 left
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days and arrange a clinic review in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy with review is the correct pathway for preseptal cellulitis, in which the globe moves freely and vision is normal. Painful restricted movement with reduced colour discrimination places this behind the orbital septum, where oral absorption and clinic follow up are both inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Arrange contrast computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses and start intravenous antibiotics with eye review
options.rationale: Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and red desaturation indicate post septal involvement, and contrast imaging is needed to identify a subperiosteal or orbital collection that would require drainage. Intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology involvement begin immediately rather than after the scan. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Apply warm compresses with topical chloramphenicol ointment and review in the short stay unit in six hours
options.rationale: Topical treatment addresses the conjunctival surface and has no effect on an infection sited within the orbit behind the septum. A six hour observation period also allows optic nerve compromise to progress unmonitored. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis before committing the child to any intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: There is no neck stiffness, altered conscious state or other feature pointing to meningeal involvement, and the localising signs all sit within the orbit. Lumbar puncture would delay treatment of the process that is actually threatening this child's vision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer directly for urgent surgical drainage of the orbit without obtaining any cross sectional imaging beforehand
options.rationale: Many children with post septal infection settle on intravenous antibiotics alone, and imaging is what distinguishes those with a drainable collection from those without. Operating without knowing whether a collection exists commits a child to an avoidable procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Infection around the eye divides at the orbital septum, and that division drives the entire management pathway. Preseptal disease produces lid swelling and erythema with a freely mobile globe, normal acuity and normal colour vision, and is treated orally in the community with review. Post septal or orbital disease adds proptosis, pain or restriction on eye movement, reduced acuity, an afferent pupillary defect or red desaturation, and is managed with admission, intravenous antibiotics, imaging and ophthalmology involvement. Ethmoid sinusitis is the usual source in school aged children because the lamina papyracea is thin and permits direct spread. The complications that justify urgency are optic nerve compromise, subperiosteal abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial extension.
key_points: The septum divides preseptal disease, treated orally, from orbital disease, which needs admission and imaging
Proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement, reduced acuity and red desaturation all indicate post septal spread
Ethmoid sinusitis spreading through the lamina papyracea is the usual source in school aged children
Contrast computed tomography identifies a subperiosteal collection and guides whether drainage is needed
Intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology review start before the scan rather than after the report
explanation.pearls: Red desaturation, tested by asking the child which eye sees a red object as brighter, becomes abnormal before visual acuity falls, so it is the earliest bedside sign that the optic nerve is under pressure.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler taking nine hundred millilitres of cow milk daily with a normal ferritin during a viral illness
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an eighteen month old boy whose mother reports that he has become pale, fussy and less interested in walking over the past two months. He is still breastfed at night and drinks around nine hundred millilitres of full cream cow milk each day from a bottle, which leaves him with little appetite for family meals.

He was born at term with no neonatal problems and has no family history of anaemia. He had a runny nose and a low grade fever three days ago which has now settled. His growth has tracked steadily along the twenty fifth centile.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae and palmar creases, soft systolic flow murmur at the left sternal edge, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 64 fL (73-85), mean cell haemoglobin 21 pg (24-30), red cell distribution width 18.4 per cent (11.5-14.5), platelets 486 x10^9/L (150-450), white cell count within normal limits, ferritin 48 mcg/L (15-200), C reactive protein 22 mg/L (less than 5), blood film shows microcytic hypochromic cells with pencil forms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral elemental iron three milligrams per kilogram daily and cap cow milk at five hundred millilitres each day
options.rationale: The film, indices and raised red cell distribution width describe iron deficiency, and the normal ferritin is explained by the raised C reactive protein, since ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant during intercurrent illness. Replacement plus reduction of the milk volume that is both displacing iron rich food and causing occult gut losses addresses cause and deficit together. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Order haemoglobin electrophoresis and defer any treatment until the pattern of haemoglobin fractions is available
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait is worth considering in a microcytic child, but it characteristically gives a normal or low red cell distribution width with a red cell count that is high for the haemoglobin, and the pencil forms here point elsewhere. Electrophoresis is also distorted by coexisting iron deficiency, so treating first and testing later is the better sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an urgent bone marrow aspirate given the degree of anaemia and the presence of a new systolic murmur
options.rationale: A flow murmur is an expected haemodynamic consequence of anaemia at this haemoglobin and is not itself a marrow indication. Normal white cells and platelets above the reference range, with no organomegaly or bruising, argue strongly against marrow infiltration. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Reassure the mother that the ferritin is normal and repeat the full blood count after the viral illness has resolved
options.rationale: This is the specific trap the C reactive protein is there to expose, because inflammation lifts ferritin into the normal range while stores remain empty. A haemoglobin of 88 g/L with a symptomatic child is not a result to observe for several weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer for an intravenous iron infusion as first line therapy because oral iron is poorly tolerated at this age
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, ongoing losses that outstrip oral intake, or documented failure of an adequately taken oral trial. Starting there exposes a well toddler to an infusion reaction risk for a deficiency that usually corrects with drops and dietary change. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers, and excessive cow milk intake is the commonest driver, acting through three mechanisms at once. Milk is low in iron, it displaces iron rich solids by filling the child, and in large volumes it causes a low grade protein losing enteropathy with occult blood loss. Volumes above about five hundred millilitres a day in this age group are the practical threshold. The diagnostic trap is that ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so any concurrent infection lifts it into the normal range and a normal value cannot exclude deficiency unless inflammatory markers are also normal. Beyond the anaemia itself, sustained iron deficiency in the second year of life is associated with lasting deficits in cognition and behaviour, which is why treatment is not deferred.
key_points: Cow milk above roughly five hundred millilitres daily in a toddler is a leading cause of iron deficiency
Ferritin rises with inflammation, so a normal value alongside a raised C reactive protein does not exclude deficiency
A high red cell distribution width with pencil forms favours iron deficiency over thalassaemia trait
Oral elemental iron at three milligrams per kilogram daily is first line, with intravenous iron reserved for failure
A soft flow murmur is an expected consequence of anaemia rather than a separate cardiac problem
explanation.pearls: Recheck the haemoglobin four weeks after starting oral iron and expect a rise of at least 10 g/L; continue treatment for a further three months after normalisation to refill stores rather than stopping once the count corrects.

subtopic_detail: Witnessed breathing pauses and morning headache in a four year old with large tonsils and poor weight gain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a four year old girl whose parents describe loud snoring on most nights since she was two. Her father has recorded a video on his phone in which she stops breathing for around twelve seconds, then gasps and rolls over.

She wakes unrefreshed, complains of headache on several mornings a week and falls asleep in the car on short trips. Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and oppositional behaviour in the afternoons. Her weight has drifted from the fiftieth to the tenth centile over eighteen months while her height has tracked steadily.

data_table.Examination: Mouth breathing at rest with hyponasal speech, tonsils meeting in the midline, no cervical lymphadenopathy, normal tympanic membranes, no adenoidal facies, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal, body mass index on the tenth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of adenotonsillectomy as the definitive treatment
options.rationale: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoea, unrefreshing sleep, daytime somnolence, neurobehavioural change and faltering weight in a child with obstructing tonsils is the clinical picture for which adenotonsillectomy is first line and curative in the large majority. Surgical referral does not require a preceding sleep study when the history and airway findings are this concordant. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray for six weeks and review the symptoms at the end of that treatment period
options.rationale: Intranasal steroid has a modest role in mild disease or in children awaiting surgery, but it does not reduce tonsillar tissue meeting in the midline. Using it as the sole strategy here accepts six more weeks of fragmented sleep in a child already losing weight centiles. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Arrange a trial of continuous positive airway pressure delivered overnight through a paediatric nasal interface
options.rationale: Positive airway pressure is reserved for children in whom surgery is contraindicated, has already failed, or who have craniofacial or neuromuscular disease, because adherence in preschoolers is poor. It treats the obstruction nightly rather than removing the tissue causing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Refer for developmental assessment of attention difficulties before pursuing any investigation of the sleep symptoms
options.rationale: Inattention and oppositional behaviour are recognised daytime consequences of fragmented sleep in this age group and commonly improve once the obstruction is relieved. Assessing attention first risks labelling a sleep disorder as a primary behavioural one. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Request overnight oximetry at home and treat only if the trace shows at least three clusters of desaturation below ninety
options.rationale: Oximetry has value when it is positive, since a positive trace confirms disease, but a negative study does not exclude it and would wrongly stand down a convincing clinical picture. Making treatment conditional on the trace inverts the relationship between a screening test and a strong history. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects around two to four per cent of Australian children and peaks between two and six years, matching the period of greatest adenotonsillar hypertrophy relative to airway size. The daytime phenotype in children differs from adults, presenting as inattention, hyperactivity and oppositionality more often than as frank sleepiness, which is why it is regularly mistaken for a primary behavioural disorder. Untreated disease carries consequences across growth, cardiovascular function and learning, with faltering growth driven by increased work of breathing and disrupted growth hormone secretion during fragmented slow wave sleep. Polysomnography remains the reference standard but access is limited in Australia, and it is not required before referral when the history and examination agree. Adenotonsillectomy resolves symptoms in the large majority of otherwise healthy children.
key_points: Peak incidence is two to six years, matching maximal adenotonsillar size relative to the airway
Daytime presentation in children is inattention and oppositionality more often than overt sleepiness
Faltering growth reflects increased work of breathing and disrupted slow wave growth hormone release
Adenotonsillectomy is first line and curative in most otherwise healthy children with concordant findings
A negative overnight oximetry trace does not exclude the diagnosis and should not override a strong history
explanation.pearls: Children under three years, those with a body mass index above the ninety fifth centile and those with trisomy 21 or neuromuscular disease need postoperative overnight monitoring after adenotonsillectomy, as their risk of respiratory compromise in the first night is materially higher.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric sleep services
